title: Working Capital: The Investment Most SMEs Don't Realise They're Making

lines: Six months ago, Ramesh nearly ran out of cash in his best month ever.
Today, the news is even better.
Sir, Sharma Retail has signed! Twenty lakh of orders, every single month!
And this time, Lata has done her homework before anyone asked.
Sir, this order will earn us about five lakh a month. But before the first rupee comes in, we will need nearly forty lakh more.
Forty lakh. Not for a new godown. Not for a new van. Just to keep the business running.
Welcome to working capital: the investment most businesses don't realise they're making.
When most people think about investment, they think about things they can see. A new machine. A delivery vehicle. An office renovation.
When Ramesh bought his van last year, everyone could see where the money went.
Working capital is different. You don't see it. You don't cut a ribbon for it. You don't announce it on social media.
Yet every business invests in it, every single day.
Think about everything Ramesh pays for before Sharma Retail pays him.
The stock is bought. The staff are paid. The godown rent is due. The trucks are loaded, and the diesel is paid for. The invoice goes out.
And only then does the customer eventually make payment.
Between spending money and receiving money, there is a gap.
Follow one rupee through Ramesh's business.
On day one, it buys stock from Kapoor, who gives thirty days' credit.
On day thirty, Ramesh pays Kapoor, and the stock goes out to Sharma Retail.
Sharma Retail pays in sixty days.
So the rupee leaves Ramesh's bank on day thirty, and comes back on day ninety. For sixty days, it is working somewhere else.
The question is not whether the cycle exists. The question is how efficiently it is being managed.
Now multiply that rupee by twenty lakh a month.
Sixty days of sales waiting with Sharma Retail: forty lakh.
One month of extra stock in the godown: fifteen lakh.
Kapoor's credit covers fifteen lakh of that.
What is left, forty lakh, has to come from Ramesh, or from his bank.
Many owners naturally assume that higher sales will automatically improve financial strength. In reality, growth often demands additional working capital.
More stock, more staff, more trucks on the road, more credit to customers, all paid for long before the money comes back.
So, in the month of his biggest order, Ramesh sits down with his bank manager to ask for a higher limit.
Not because the business was failing. Because the business was growing.
Here is what most owners miss. Working capital is not a number the accountant finds at month-end.
It is created by decisions made all over the business: in sales, in purchase, in dispatch and in collections.
Sir, Sharma Retail is asking for ninety days instead of sixty.
Thirty more days of credit on twenty lakh a month: another twenty lakh waiting.
Ramesh bhai, take three months' stock now, and I'll give you two percent off.
Two percent off sounds good. It also puts thirty lakh more on Ramesh's shelves.
A truck held up for a week means an invoice raised a week late, and cash a week late.
Rameshji, you know my payment is always safe. Next month, definitely.
Thirty days late on fifteen lakh: fifteen lakh more, waiting.
What appears in the financial statements is often the result of decisions being made throughout the business.
Lata does not run a complicated formula. Every Monday, she asks four questions.
How much stock are we carrying?
Are we buying more than we need?
How long does a rupee take to come back?
Those questions usually reveal more than a spreadsheet ever will.
So Ramesh holds Sharma Retail at sixty days.
He thanks Kapoor, and buys one month's stock, not three.
And he arranges the bank limit before the first truck leaves, not on a Friday afternoon in a panic.
Three months later, Sharma Retail's payments start arriving, on time. Salaries went out on the first of every month.
Sir, same order, same profit. The only difference is that this time, we knew the money would be away for sixty days.

Working capital is not idle money. It is not excess cash sitting in a bank account. It is the fuel that allows operations to continue between the moment money is spent and the moment money is received.
Because in the end, working capital is simply the cost of keeping the wheels turning.
